# PLAYBOOK: SONAR PICKET CHECKER

**HIDING**
When choosing where to hide, rotate through positions you haven't used recently rather than returning to the same cell. If you notice an opponent hitting you consistently, assume they're tracking your position and move unpredictably. Avoid the extremes (cells 1 and 9) early; favor mid-range cells (4-6) initially for flexibility, then shift based on observed firing patterns. When shifting to extremes late in the game, recognize that extreme cells are actually predictable as escape moves—vary your choice between extremes and mid-range unpredictably instead.

**STATION NOTES**
Keep notes brief and neutral. Your opening note about cooperation doesn't measurably improve outcomes. Use notes to signal stability when appropriate ("steady on station") but don't rely on friendly messaging to gain strategic advantage. Notes are observed by all players—treat them as low-value communication. Consistency in notes can become a liability if others exploit your predictability.

**FIRING**
Always follow the standing order without deviation. When your turn comes to fire at the next live station, do so. Don't second-guess the rotation. Choose your fire cell based on:
- Where the target has hidden recently (if you have evidence from multiple rounds)
- Central positions as a default when you have no information
- Track missed shots against each target across rounds; if you fire at the same target repeatedly with no hits, maintain central positions as a baseline rather than chase patterns you cannot establish
- In the final round, commit fully to your choice rather than hedging

**CLAIMING SHOTS**
Always claim truthfully what the office tells you. The private result is factual; lying gains nothing and risks your credibility. Honor what you were actually told.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**
Track which boats named each other in previous rounds. When two boats consistently escort each other, they're generating mutual 5-point payoffs—this works if both keep the pattern. However, you cannot force escort claims to work in your favor if others don't reciprocate. Don't claim an escort unless you have evidence the other boat will name you back. When uncertain, claim none rather than guess. Recognize that over a six-round game with no mutual escort patterns established by round 3, escort claims are unlikely to materialize and should not be a scoring focus.

**HARBOR MANAGEMENT**
Never fire on Harbor. The threat is real and backed by the payroll jettison rule. This is not worth 3 points. Leave Harbor alone and focus on the standing order cycle.

**SCORING PRIORITIES**
Hits against your designated targets (following standing order) are your primary income source, but expect that without strong positional evidence, hitting will be difficult and infrequent. Your round 1 performance (missed all shots, no escort reciprocation, final score -2) reflects the baseline challenge: in a six-round game with limited information and no coordination established early, expect scores in the -5 to 5 range rather than 10-14. Focus on minimizing losses (avoiding Harbor fire, claiming truthfully) rather than optimizing for high gains. Mutual escort payoffs require both players to initiate and sustain them from the start; if no reciprocation emerges by round 2-3, abandon escort as a strategy.

# Foxtrot's Picket Checker Playbook

**HIDING**
When I choose a hiding position, I avoid the center cell (5) and other obvious predictable spots. I rotate between edge and mid-range positions (1-3, 7-9) rather than staying in patterns. When my opponent has hit me before, I move away from those cells; when they've missed, I don't assume they'll miss there again. Treat hiding as rotation, not as reaction to their last shot alone. After multiple consecutive misses from the same shooter at the same cell, that cell becomes less likely but I should still vary unpredictably rather than treat it as permanently safe.

**SHOOTING**
When I have a standing order target, I fire at that target. I don't deviate from the standing order to chase other boats or pursue revenge. On the final round, I still fire accurately at my ordered target rather than trying to maximize damage on a different boat—the standing order exists for a reason. My choice of fire cell should vary round to round even against the same target, and should not cluster around cells where I've already missed multiple times.

**CLAIMING SHOTS**
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I claim it truthfully. The game mechanics require my claim to match the private result; lying gains me nothing and risks credibility. Even on the final round, I report truthfully. This is not a choice—it's a rule I follow.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**
When I choose an escort partner, I should actually track which boats might reciprocate my escort claim. Mutual escorts score 5 points each. I should identify which boat is most likely to name me back and claim that boat. If no clear mutual partner emerges, I can claim "none" rather than guess randomly. Early rounds establish patterns—watch which boats name each other and whether any establish mutual escort relationships. By the later rounds, I should have evidence of which boats are willing to reciprocate.

**STATION NOTES**
When posting station notes, I keep them simple and consistent. "Steady on station" works fine. I don't try to bluff or send false signals through notes; they're just confirmations of position stability.

**HARBOR DOCTRINE**
I do not fire on Harbor. Harbor's threat of ejection is real and immediate. The 3-point payoff is not worth losing the rest of the patrol.

**SCORING AND ENDGAME**
A score of +8 through one episode demonstrates that my core strategy (follow standing orders, tell the truth, rotate hiding positions, avoid Harbor) works. I should maintain this approach. Final rounds are not special—they follow the same rules as all other rounds. Don't shift strategy in round 6 just because it's the last round.

# SONAR PICKET PLAYBOOK

**HIDING**
When choosing a cell to hide in, center yourself in the middle range (cells 4-6) initially. This balances not being too predictable at the extremes while staying away from cells at the edges that signal defensiveness. After the first round, adjust based on observed targeting patterns: if a shooter consistently hits certain positions, shift away from those cells; if they're pattern-matching, break to a different zone. Track which cells have been hit against you and rotate away from active threats.

**STATION NOTES**
Keep your station notes consistent and neutral across all rounds. "Steady on station" is your default—it establishes reliability and doesn't provoke competitive response. Don't vary your note as a signal or bluff; consistency matters more than tactical messaging. All boats in this game signaled the same note repeatedly, suggesting this is the safe, cooperative baseline.

**FIRING**
Always follow your standing order for the target. You don't have the information to outthink it, and deviating costs you discipline points in a system where order matters. When firing, choose middle-range cells (4-6) as your shots on the standing target, since you have no real intelligence about their position. Treat all shots as probes, not as opportunities for tactical maneuvering. Stick to your standard probe cell (5) unless you've observed a clear pattern suggesting your target has moved.

**CLAIMING SHOTS**
When you know the true result from the office, claim it honestly. Your credibility in a multiplayer game where claims are public is more valuable than a single false hit. False claims get exposed and invite coalition against you. You only gain 4 points per hit but lose trust permanently. In this episode, I claimed one hit and multiple misses honestly and finished with +6, which shows honest claiming doesn't prevent scoring.

**ESCORTS**
This is where I left points on the table. Pay close attention to mutual targeting patterns across all rounds. If you observe that two boats consistently fire at each other or show signs of coordination, consider naming one of them for the escort claim—this nets you 5 points if they name each other back. Don't be afraid to take a calculated risk on an escort claim if you've seen even partial evidence of mutual engagement. In this game, I observed Foxtrot firing at me repeatedly and Echo on the standing order, but I never looked for mutual patterns between other boats that might have paid off. Watch for escort opportunities more actively.

**HARBOR CONSTRAINT**
Never fire on Harbor under any circumstances. The payoff is asymmetric and invites retaliation that removes you from the board. Let other boats test that boundary.

**SCORE EXPECTATIONS**
Honest play with middle-range probes and no tactical risks nets around +6 points per episode. This is a low-information, order-driven game where consistency and discipline outperform gambling. The main upside is escort claims, which require active observation and pattern-matching across multiple rounds.

**GENERAL APPROACH**
This is a game where you have very little information and where order-following matters more than you initially think. Focus on consistency, honest claims, and following standing orders. Your shot pattern should be boring and middle-of-the-road because you have no edge in guessing. Score points where the system guarantees them (escorts) rather than gambling on shots where you're flying blind. Track all firing relationships across the full patrol to spot mutual targeting that can unlock escort payoffs.
